author: Julius Gavroche
title: A man died today in Ceuta
content:
On the 30th to the 31st of July, over 70,000 people crossed the Moroccan border into Ceuta, a Spanish territory adjacent to the African country. After the return to Morocco of most of those who crossed, some 10,000 people still 

remain in Ceuta

 in precarious conditions, subject to all manner of deprivations and violence, predictable and unpredictable.







from 

lundimatin

 #535, 28/09/2026




A man died today, Friday 25 September 2026, in Ceuta, near the showers at Playa del Trampolín.







Of Algerian origin and in his fifties, he collapsed in this area where, for nearly two months now, men who have arrived in Ceuta have been living. Paramedics attempted to resuscitate him for more than twenty minutes. He died at the scene. It was reported that he had been unwell for several days.




Since the end of July, men have been living in Trampolín in precarious conditions that are by no means accidental. They sleep on the beach, behind the rocks or against the walls of the old factory, in shelters made of tarpaulins, cardboard and pieces of wood. They wash in makeshift showers, rely on food handouts and, day by day, scour for the essentials they need to get by: water, a few items of clothing, a socket to charge a phone, a place to sleep without being evicted.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: The political topography of anarchism
content:
Olaus Magnus, detail from 

Carta Marina

, 1539




On old maps, it is common to see areas populated by mythological creatures, mermaids and Amazons, dragons and unicorns. The beings that inhabit the most remote and unexplored regions – those known or presumed to exist, but which are not yet understood – are depicted in great detail. The accounts of the few travellers who have reached these places are passed on by word of mouth and become distorted as they are retold; they are magnified and exaggerated, until from a narrative—presumed to be more or less reliable—an entire imaginary topography emerges, which serves at the same time to prove the existence of the mythical creatures whose territory it delineates. The circular reasoning is evident.  Dragons exist because they live there, at the edge of the world. This places them on the map. And they live there because they exist and must be somewhere. That is why they can feature in the depiction of the world.







Similarly, in the nineteenth century, with the fantastical excesses of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance now a thing of the past, Victorian explorers – salacot hats on their heads and rifles at the ready – set about methodically filling in the gaps that still remained on the maps. author: Julius Gavroche
title: Opening essay/An effort at an openning: The State, the people, the strategist
content:
from 

lundimatin

 #533, 15/09/2026







This is often the case during election campaigns, and it is probably even more so given the rise of fascist tendencies: everything is put on hold – common sense, reality, boldness, autonomy, determination. Instead, people sound out the situation, calculate their moves, whisper little secrets in each other’s ears and spout posturing that rings hollow. Everyone thinks they are manipulating everyone else, but it is always reality that we are scheming with. The author of this text sets out to examine what this appetite for political manoeuvring entails. Spoiler: the very logic of a world it purports to criticise.







Every political strategy, whatever its political persuasion, is based on two key concepts: the sovereign subject and the state apparatus. Whichever side it takes, it implies intervention from the outside into the structures. Whether they aim to prevent the decline of the white race or ward off the coming of fascism, political strategies rest on the same hackneyed fiction: the political – 

subject

. The fact that their aims are opposite changes nothing of their form. One hates what the other defends, but both call upon a subject to rise up, a people to count themselves, a mass to allow itself to be led. Yet there is no subject, any more than there is an object. title: Peregrination: Foreignness/Strangeness/Otherness as a counterpower
content:
Jörg Breu the Elder,

, 1500




from 

Ficcíon de la rázon

Peregrinatio. La extrañeza como contrapoder




Federico Ferrari




We have been taken in by the hypnotic fable of the apocalypse. Public discourse, intoxicated by the spectacle of imminent ruin and by the narcissism of catastrophe, continues to tell us that we are living through the end of time. An end that drags on indefinitely, like a well-structured Netflix series in which the epilogue is always postponed to the next episode. In reality, the mass apocalyptic narrative is nothing more than a form of anaesthetic: it serves to mask the only true tragedy of the present, namely that 

nothing changes

 in the great continuum of the history of oppression and that things continue to slide, without the slightest disruption, along the tracks of their political and social collapse.







However, beneath the ashes of this spectacle of ruin, something profoundly new has taken root. What we must come to terms with today, in Italy and at the heart of Europe, is not merely the continuation of the ruthless violence of classical liberalism, nor even a straightforward reproduction of the historical fascisms of the twentieth century. author: Julius Gavroche
title: Remembering John Coltrane (1926-1967)
content:
Little of beauty has America given the world save the rude grandeur God himself stamped on her bosom; the human spirit in this new world has expressed itself in vigor and ingenuity rather than in beauty. And so by fateful chance the Negro folk-song—the rhythmic cry of the slave—stands to-day not simply as the sole American music, but as the most beautiful expression of human experience born this side the seas. It has been neglected, it has been, and is, half despised, and above all it has been persistently mistaken and misunderstood; but notwithstanding, it still remains as the singular spiritual heritage of the nation and the greatest gift of the Negro people.




W.E.B. Du Bois, 

The Souls of Black Folk

, 1903




Whenever I make a change, I’m a little worried that it may puzzle people. And sometimes I deliberately delay things for this reason. But after a while I find there is nothing else I can do but go ahead.

title: Against the Tide
content:
from 

New Left Review-Sidecar

, 

18/09/2026







by Morten Høi Jensen




Prospective biographers of Victor Serge begin at a disadvantage. 

Memoirs of a Revolutionary

 (1951) is one of the great autobiographies of the last century, vividly recounting the twists and turns – from Belgium to France, Spain, Russia, Mexico – of a spectacularly dramatic political life. Yet as Mitchell Abidor argues in his recent biography, Serge’s story ‘is more complex than his memoirs would lead the reader to believe’. 

Victor Serge: Unruly Revolutionary

 aims to ‘roughen edges’ that the memoirist smoothed over and probe ‘contradictions’ that he minimized. Begun as an attempt to help Richard Greeman complete his own, never completed biography of Serge, Abidor’s account draws on the astonishing archive of material Greeman spent a lifetime assembling. While Suzi Weissman’s impassioned 

Victor Serge: A Political Biography

 (2001) was written to rescue Serge’s legacy from post-Cold War triumphalism, Abidor offers a cooler and more sceptical account, leaving no ideological inconsistency unexamined.

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Isaac Deutscher: Message of the Non-Jewish Jew
content:
The following article by the biographer of Stalin and Trotsky, whose writings on Russia and Eastern Europe appear regularly in periodicals throughout the world, is based on a lecture delivered in London last February during Jewish Book Week to the World Jewish Congress. This text, revised and extended by the author, appeared in 

Universities and Left Review

, and is reprinted here with the author’s permission. A summary of the lecture had previously appeared in the British 

Jewish Observer and Middle East Review.







I REMEMBER that when as a child I read the 

Midrash

 I came across a story and a description of a scene which gripped my imagination. It was the story of Rabbi Meir, the great saint, sage, and the pillar of Mosaic orthodoxy and co-author of the 

Mishna

, who took lessons in theology from a heretic Elisha ben Abiyuh, nicknamed Akher (The Stranger). Once on a Sabbath, Rabbi Meir went out on a trip with his teacher, and as usual they became engaged in deep argument. The heretic was riding a donkey, and Rabbi Meir, as he could not ride on a Sabbath, walked by his side and listened so intently to the words of wisdom falling from heretical lips, that he failed to notice that he and his teacher had reached the ritual boundary which Jews were not allowed to cross on a Sabbath. content:

Marking 350 years since the death of the English revolutionary Digger (1609-1676)




Robert Graham, Illustrations: Clifford Harper




During the peak of Gerrard Winstanley’s political activity in 1649-1650, he championed an early form of anarchist communism using a radical Protestant vernacular. Winstanley denounced coercive government (“government by the sword”) and private property (“mine and thine”), and through non-violent direct action sought to create egalitarian communities where everything would be held in common.







In his first explicitly political pamphlet, 

The New Law of Righteousness 

(1649), Winstanley argued that the desire to dominate and exploit others for one’s own advantage results not only in the creation of government, or “rule and dominion,” so that “one part of man-kind” may rule “over another,” but that it is through this hierarchical rule that private property is established, “thereby restraining other fellow creatures from seeking nourishment from their mother earth,” which the rich and powerful have claimed as their own.

title: Repression and Resistance in Russia: An Overview
content:

Across three decades, Russia has been at the forefront of the worldwide 

descent into authoritarianism

. Vladimir Putin’s government has suppressed opposition in ways that aspiring autocrats like Donald Trump are still striving to emulate. Yet despite widespread repression, there is still resistance in Russia, and as Putin’s model proliferates, people everywhere around the world stand to benefit from learning about it. Likewise, we should support Russian anarchist and 

anti-war

 prisoners, both because resistance within Russia offers hope for the eventual end of war and totalitarianism and because, should autocrats consolidate power where we live, we will wish for people to support us, as well.

Baltic Anarchist Book Fair
